title: collapse_index on a broken index gives difficult-to-debug errors
description:
Hi,

This is really feedback from an 'I shot myself in the foot and spent ages working out why/how' thing. I don't have a reprex per se - I suspect one could be made if I think about it for long enough...Apologies that I haven't had time to explore the issue further (yet).

I managed to produce a broken tibbletime index. The way I think I did this was by left joining two tibbletime tables. Because the tables started out with the same name, I renamed the index on the LHS before joining (so far so good - so our intended index is on the LHS with a new name, and the old index on the RHS has the original name and is still present but now may contain NULLs).

However I then tried to call dplyr::mutate with collapse_index on the old index name to make the collapsed index field by mistake rather than the new name.

The error you get is: Error in mutate_impl(.data, dots) : 
  Evaluation error: missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed.

Clearly that is a long way away from where the error truly lies (ie. using an invalid index).

My thoughts:
- Is this an issue with joining two tibbletime tables with valid indices? Is the index on the RHS invalidated (ie. no longer recognised as a tibbletime index) as it should?
- Is this possible with a non-indexed date/time field containing NULLs? Would that result in the same error? Or would collapse_index spot that we're using an invalid index in those circumstances?
- If collapse_index is able to work on any columns (which I doubt), does collapse_index need to check for the presence of NULLs before working, and give a more descriptive error?

Hope this makes sense. If I get the time I'll try to make a reprex for you of this is in action if it doesn't make sense from the above!

description:

I understand tibbletime objects are indexed by date-time. Could indices be redone with remaining index values when `drop_na` is used? 

Here's an example of what's happening:


![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/7339049/87274186-26576400-c4a9-11ea-81c3-c853b90e3d72.png)
Clearly here `drop_na()` could been done before casting `df` to tibbletime object. But in a practical world for instance, the original `df` object could've been used for plotting all values of individual series. Then NA values could've been dropped downstream for computing portfolio returns, which in this case would require recasting `df` to a tibbletime object again, if its properties were to be used.

title: Add rollify for irregular time series
description:
I would like to add a version of rollify for irregular time series. Something like the code below works and can be called like this:

`rollify_time(mean, window = 2, lag = 1)(x = 1:8, date_time = c(1, 2, 3, 3, 3.5, 4, 5, 7))`

I will submit a PR but I wanted to see whether I should merge this function with `rollify` so that `rollify` can be called like

`rollify(mean, date_time = my_time_var, window = 2, lag = 1)(x = 1:8, my_time_var = c(1, 2, 3, 3, 3.5, 4, 5, 7))`

The default argument for `date_time` would be `NULL` so if you wanted to call `rollify` as before it would be:

`rollify(mean, window = 2)(x = 1:8)`

```
rollify_time <- function(.f, window = 1, lag = 0, unlist = TRUE, na_value = NULL) {

  # Mappify the function
  .f <- purrr::as_mapper(.f)

  # Return function that calls roller
  function(..., date_time) {
    roller_time(..., date_time = date_time, .f = .f, window = window, lag = lag,
           unlist = unlist, na_value = na_value)
  }
}

roller_time <- function(..., date_time, .f, window, lag, unlist = TRUE, na_value = NULL) {

  # na_value as NA if not specified
  if(is.null(na_value)) {
    na_value = NA
  }

  # Capture dots as list. These should be the arguments that are rolled
  .dots <- rlang::dots_list(...)

  # Error check the dots
  check_dots_time(.dots, date_time, lag)

  # Each data element of .dots should be of the same length so use the first
  # as the length of the dataset
  roll_length <- length(.dots[[1]])

  # Initialize `filled` vector
  filled <- rlang::rep_along(1:roll_length, list(na_value))

  window_min <- 1
  window_max <- 2
  start_index <- which.max(date_time - lag >= date_time[1])

  # Roll and fill
  for(i in start_index:roll_length) {
    while (date_time[i] - window - lag >= date_time[window_min]) {
      window_min <- window_min + 1
    }

    while (window_max <= roll_length & date_time[i] - lag >= date_time[window_max]) {
      window_max <- window_max + 1
    }

    .f_dots <- lapply(.dots, function(x) {
      x[window_min:(window_max - 1)]
    })
    filled[[i]] <- do.call(.f, .f_dots)
  }

  # Don't unlist if requested (when >1 value returned)
  if(unlist) {
    unlist(filled)
  } else {
    filled
  }

}

# Check that dots follow the necessary convention for rolling
check_dots_time <- function(x, date_time, lag) {

  # The user must have passed something to be passed on to .f
  assertthat::assert_that(length(x) > 0,
                          msg = "At least 1 data argument must be supplied to be
                          passed on to the rolling function")

  # The lag must be smaller than the time range of the data
```

description:

```
10 2008-01-15  3.23  3.31  2.96  3.15 37895200.     3.15       3.15
# ... with 2,555 more rows
```

Here's the code I'm using to get it done. Three basic functions:

1. `prep_tbl_time()` - helper function to automatically convert to `tbl_time` - Identifying the time index was getting a bit repetitive.
2. `time_frequency()` -  A really useful function that is helping to work between `tbl_time` and `ts`. The frequency is automatically calculated using `collapse_by()`. It's a different approach that makes more intuitive frequency calculations.
3. `time_apply()` - The workhorse function that applies a function across (1) a numeric span, (2) a character span using `collapse_by()`, or (3) and automatically selected frequency based on the estimated frequency from `time_frequency(period = "auto")`. 

```
library(tidyverse)
library(tidyquant)
library(timetk)
library(tibbletime)

prep_tbl_time <- function(data, message = TRUE) {
    if(!"tbl_time" %in% class(data)) {
        if (message) message(glue("Converting from {class(data)[[1]]} to tbl_time"))
        data <- data %>% 
            as_tbl_time(index = !! rlang::sym(tk_get_timeseries_variables(.)[[1]]))
    }
    return(data)
}

time_frequency <- function(data, period = "auto", message = TRUE) {
    
    # Setup inputs
    data <- prep_tbl_time(data, message = F)
    
    index_expr <- data %>% get_index_quo()
    index_name <- quo_name(index_expr)
    
    # Get timeseries summary attributes
    ts_summary <- data %>%
        get_index_col() %>%
        tk_get_timeseries_summary()
    
    ts_nobs  <- ts_summary$n.obs
    ts_scale <- ts_summary$scale
    
    
    if (is.numeric(period)) {
        # 1. Numeric Periods
        freq <- period
        
    } else if (period != "auto") {
        # 2. Text (e.g. period = "2 Weeks")
        freq <- data %>%
            collapse_by(period = period) %>%
            count(!! index_expr) %>%
            pull(n) %>%
            median(na.rm = T)
        
    } else {
        # 3. period = "auto"
        
        # ts_scales: 
        ts_scales_tbl <- tk_get_timeseries_unit_frequency() %>% 
            gather() %>%
            mutate(
                resolution = ifelse(value <= 3600, "high", "low"),
                lead_1 = dplyr::lead(key, n = 1),
                lead_2 = dplyr::lead(key, n = 2)
            ) %>%
            tidyr::fill(lead_1, lead_2, .direction = "down") %>%
            mutate(
                target = ifelse(resolution == "high", lead_1, lead_2)
            ) %>%
            select(-c(lead_1, lead_2))
        
        # Frequency calculation: get target frequency from scale
        target_freq_scale <- function(scale, index_shift = 0) {
            
            idx <- which(ts_scales_tbl$key == scale) - index_shift
            key_value <- ts_scales_tbl$key[idx]
            
            ts_scales_tbl %>%
                filter(key == key_value) %>%
                pull(target)
        }
        
        periodicity_target <- target_freq_scale(ts_scale)
        
        freq <- data %>%
            collapse_by(period = periodicity_target) %>%
            count(!! index_expr) %>%
            pull(n) %>%
            median(na.rm = T)
        
        # Insufficient observations: nobs-to-freq should be at least 3-1
        if (ts_nobs < 3*freq) {
            periodicity_target <- target_freq_scale(ts_scale, index_shift = 1)
            
            freq <- data %>%
                collapse_by(period = periodicity_target) %>%
                count(!! index_expr) %>%
                pull(n) %>%
                median(na.rm = T)
        } 
        
        if (ts_nobs < 3*freq) {
            freq <- 1
        }
    }
    
    if (message) {
        freq_string <- glue("Frequency used is {freq} {ts_scale}s")
        message(freq_string)
    }
    
    return(freq)
}


time_apply <- function(data, target, period = "auto", .f, ..., 
                       start_date = NULL, side = "end", clean = FALSE, message = TRUE) {
    
    # Setup inputs
    data <- prep_tbl_time(data, message = F)
    
    date_col_expr <- get_index_quo(data)
    date_col_name <- quo_name(date_col_expr)
    
    target_expr <- enquo(target)
    
    # For median_span = "auto", no more than 12 data points in a median group
    if (period == "auto") {
        frequency <- time_frequency(data)
        time_scale <- data %>%
            get_index_col() %>%
            tk_get_timeseries_summary() %>%
            pull(scale)
        period <- glue("{frequency} {time_scale}s")
        if (message) message(glue("Auto period = {period}"))
    }
    
    # Function apply logic
    if (is.character(period)) {
        # See collapse_by for valid character sequences (e.g. "1 Y")
        ret <- data %>%
            collapse_by(period = period, clean = clean, start_date = start_date, side = side) %>%
            group_by(!! get_index_quo(.)) %>%
            mutate(time_apply = .f(!! target_expr, ...)) %>%
            ungroup() %>%
            mutate(!! date_col_name := data %>% pull(!! date_col_expr)) 
        
    } else {
        # Numeric (e.g. 15 spans)
        ret <- data %>%
            mutate(
                .period_groups = rep(1:period, length.out = nrow(.)) %>% sort()
            ) %>%
            group_by(.period_groups) %>%
            mutate(
                time_apply = .f(!! target_expr, ...)
            ) %>%
            ungroup() %>%
            select(-.period_groups)
    }
    
    return(ret)
    
}

tq_get("NFLX") %>% 
    time_apply(adjusted, period = "weekly", clean = F, .f = median, na.rm = T) 

```

title: .index synonym for referencing the index
description:
Hi,
Thanks for the package. You seem to be using different techniques to refer to index in different situations inside functions. Sometimes you simply quote it as symbol (like `index_sym` in `time_summarize`), sometimes you even `dplyr::pull()` it and make it available as vector (like in `index_raw` in `time_filter`).

Wouldn't it be nice to let users safely use `.index` to refer to the index column without ever worrying about the underlying name of the index column?

```
FANG %>% as_tbl_time(index=date) %>%
     mutate(birthday=ifelse(.index==as.Date("2013-01-07"), "my birthday!", "yet another day"))
```

Perhaps `as_tbl_time()` here should also refer to it as `.index` for consistency, but I don't have a strong opinion about it. 

This may actually simplify the interface somewhat. You may not need to provide as many wrappers for standard tidyverse functions, as user can can specify the index manipulation explicitly.

title: Daylight Savings causing grouping issues in time_summarize, time_collapse, and time_group
description:
**tl:dr** Daylight Savings is causing `create_series` to select the wrong breakpoints for `1~d` period to be used for grouping

<hr>

I have been working with `time_summarise` recently for sub-daily data (2-minute interval) to try and take daily averages. It seems that `time_summarize` is taking the values from the first hour (12:00-12:59 AM) of the following day and grouping it with the previous day. It consequently is then ignored from the day it should be with. This behavior is, however, not consistent. With some days correctly grouping the day with the last value being in the last hour of that day (11:00-11:59 PM). I have put together a small example to help illustrate the problem using hourly data and your `create_series` function.

    # first create the hourly series and add a random variable to summarize
    x <- create_series(2016-03-12 ~ 2016-03-15, period = 1~h) %>%
      mutate(random_val = 1:nrow(x),
         
             # I do this so that the break is not right at midnight
             # I would expect that it should still classify 12:00 AM as
             # the following day, but I wanted to show that that is not 
             # the only occurance
             date = date + minutes(10))

Now before diving in too deep, let me show you what I mean. 

    x_sum <- x %>%
      time_summarise(1~d, 
                     mean = mean(random_val),
                     count = n())

    x_sum

    # A time tibble: 4 x 3
    # Index: date
                     date  mean count
    *              <dttm> <dbl> <int>
    1 2016-03-12 23:10:00  12.5    24
    2 2016-03-14 00:10:00  36.5    24
    3 2016-03-15 00:10:00  60.5    24
    4 2016-03-15 23:10:00  84.0    23

As you can see, for `2016-03-12` it grouped the values correctly, with 24 values and the final time being `2016-03-12 23:10:00` (the last hourly value for that day). But that is where things get weird. For the next day (`2016-03-13`), it groups the values but includes `2016-03-14 00:10:00` in the group, which results in the date displayed to be both misleading and the subsequent summaries to be incorrect. Interestingly, `2016-03-13 00:02:00` was daylight savings time. So there are only 23 values for that day in the created dataset.
    
    x %>%
      time_filter(~2016-03-13) %>%
      ungroup() %>%
      summarize(count = n(),
                first = first(date),
                last = last(date))

    # A tibble: 1 x 3
      count               first                last
      <int>              <dttm>              <dttm>
    1    23 2016-03-13 00:10:00 2016-03-13 23:10:00

To verify this, we can look at the number of values in the tibble for just `2016-03-13` and we can indeed see that there are 23 and that the first and last value of that day are `2016-03-13 00:10:00` and the last time is `2016-03-13 23:10:00`, as would be expected. This behavior is carried on until the final day in this example, with `2016-03-15` having only 23 values, since its midnight value is placed in another group. 

To compare what it looks like using pure `dplyr`, and to confirm (at least I think this confirms it) that this is not an issue with my computers local time zones or anything like that:

    x %>%
      mutate(date_mut = date(date)) %>%
      group_by(date_mut) %>%
      summarize(last = last(date),
                mean = mean(random_val),
                count = n())

    # A tibble: 4 x 4
        date_mut                last  mean count
          <date>              <dttm> <dbl> <int>
    1 2016-03-12 2016-03-12 23:10:00  12.5    24
    2 2016-03-13 2016-03-13 23:10:00  36.0    23
    3 2016-03-14 2016-03-14 23:10:00  59.5    24
    4 2016-03-15 2016-03-15 23:10:00  83.5    24

So it looks like the pure `dplyr` method worked judging solely by the `count` and the `last` columns. Quick mean calculations, not included here, also show the `mean` column is correct. 

Now, I have tried to dive into your code to figure out where the problem could be occuring, to try and save you guys some time. It looks like [`time_summarise`](https://github.com/business-science/tibbletime/blob/master/R/time_summarise.R#L72) is a `time_collapse`, `group_by`, `summarize` combo. So I backed up and just ran `time_collapse` to see if the issue was seen there.
 
    x_col <- x %>%
      time_collapse(1~d, as_sep_col = TRUE) 

    x_col[c(23, 24, 25, 46, 47, 48),]

    # A time tibble: 6 x 3
    # Index: date
                     date               .date random_val
    *              <dttm>              <dttm>      <int>
    1 2016-03-12 23:10:00 2016-03-12 22:10:00         23
    2 2016-03-12 23:10:00 2016-03-12 23:10:00         24
    3 2016-03-14 00:10:00 2016-03-13 00:10:00         25
    4 2016-03-14 00:10:00 2016-03-13 22:10:00         46
    5 2016-03-14 00:10:00 2016-03-13 23:10:00         47
    6 2016-03-14 00:10:00 2016-03-14 00:10:00         48

As we can see, the problem does occur within `time_collapse`, and is just carried forward into `time_summarize`. Looking through the [`time_collapse`](https://github.com/business-science/tibbletime/blob/master/R/time_collapse.R#L90) code, it looks like the issue is with the `time_group` function. 

    x_tg <- x %>% 
      mutate(.time_group = time_group(date, 1~d))


    x_tg[c(23, 24, 25, 46, 47, 48),]

    # A time tibble: 6 x 3
    # Index: date
                     date random_val .time_group
    *              <dttm>      <int>       <dbl>
    1 2016-03-12 22:10:00         23           1
    2 2016-03-12 23:10:00         24           1
    3 2016-03-13 00:10:00         25           2
    4 2016-03-13 22:10:00         46           2
    5 2016-03-13 23:10:00         47           2
    6 2016-03-14 00:10:00         48           2

As we can see, `time_group` is incorrectly grouping the first hour of `2016-03-14` with `2016-03-13`. Digging into the `time_group` code is looks like the issue is at the [`create_series`](https://github.com/business-science/tibbletime/blob/master/R/time_group.R#L115) function call. Running through the function step by step on my machine with `x$date` as my index and `1~d` as my period, `endpoint_dates` is :

    [1] "2016-03-12 00:00:00 EST" "2016-03-13 00:00:00 EST" "2016-03-14 01:00:00 EDT" "2016-03-15 01:00:00 EDT"
    [5] "2016-03-16 01:00:00 EDT"
    
So it looks like for some reason this is reading 1 AM as the start of each day for `2016-03-14` through `2016-03-16`. Doing this for an extended perioed shows that the behavior persists until the end of the range since there is not data for the following day. So it seems that daylight savings is throwing off this calculation which is then affecting every subsequent calculation.

I hope this helps you nail down where the problem is. I will look at `create_series` myself to see if I come up with any creative solutions. I believe my coworker ran into an issue with monthly summaries as well, so I will look into that and let you know if I am able to reporduce it. 

Let me know if you need anything else from me, I am happy to help in any way I can.

title: time_summarise / ability to filter by periods and to have the ability to set start of period
description:
This is my second request:

In Australia our financial year starts 1/July to 30/June. Some large listed companies have financial year end in September. So to have the ability to set the start and end of financial years is useful.

It would also be super useful to have the ability to filter by "Q1" or "H1".

Background to my request:
I worked for a US listed company in Australia
All our reporting to the US was based on calendar years, so Q1 = Jan-Mar
When reporting to local regulatory bodies and for tender submissions we reported in Australian Financial year, so Q1 = Jul-Sep
Trying to organise the data in quarters/half-yearly for reporting between US and local requirements was a real nuisance and a lot time was spent checking to make sure the correct time periods were being reported.

Now if there was the ability to (1) define Financial year periods and (2) to search based on aggregates, such as Q1 life would have been oh so easy.

Is this something that you could consider building into the library.

Thanks in advance.
Kind regards,
Joe
